facts.text: On this date in 1783, the first untethered human balloon flight lifted off from Paris — making France the birthplace of aviation a full 120 years before the Wright Brothers.
On this date in 1877, Thomas Edison announced the phonograph in New York. The device was so unexpected, the French Academy of Sciences initially declared the demonstration a ventriloquist's trick.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka, Bangladesh than in the entire continent of Australia — roughly 170 million within 200 kilometers.
Indonesia spans a wider longitude than the continental United States, yet it has compressed itself into just three time zones to simplify national coordination.
The city of Istanbul is simultaneously the largest city in Europe and in Asia — the Bosphorus strait runs directly through its urban core, splitting one metropolis between two continents.
On this day in 1980, silver hit $50 an ounce as the Hunt brothers cornered the market — a price not sustainably surpassed for over 30 years.
On November 21, 1974, Franklin National Bank collapsed — then the largest U.S. bank failure in history, undone by foreign exchange speculation.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792. The original agreement had just 24 signatories and fit on a single page.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway began as a failing textile mill. He later called buying it the worst investment of his life — a $200B mistake in opportunity cost.
Japan's Nikkei 225 peaked on December 29, 1989 at 38,957. It took 35 years to reclaim that level, the longest major index recovery in modern financial history.

On this date in 1905, Einstein submitted his paper on special relativity. Time dilation it describes isn't theoretical: GPS satellites must correct their clocks by 38 microseconds daily or navigation errors accumulate at 10km per day.

On November 21, 1783, humans first flew — in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon over Paris. The passengers brought a pile of straw and a bucket of water, convinced they could manually control altitude by managing the flame.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.

Your body replaces its entire skeleton approximately every 10 years. Bone is living tissue constantly dissolving and rebuilding — the femur you broke as a child no longer contains a single original atom.
The universe is not expanding into anything. Space itself is stretching, and distant galaxies aren't moving through space — the space between you and them is simply growing.
On this day in 1783, humans first flew — Pilâtre de Rozier drifted over Paris in a hot air balloon. The US Constitution was still four years away.
Fax machines predate the telephone. Alexander Bain patented his 'electric printing telegraph' in 1843, over 30 years before Bell made his first call.
On this day in 1877, Edison announced the phonograph — a machine to preserve the dead's voices. Victorian newspapers called it 'the most wonderful invention of the age.'
The woolly mammoth was still alive when the Great Pyramid was being built. The last isolated herd died on Wrangel Island around 1650 BC, centuries into Egyptian civilization.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire by roughly 300 years. Lectures began there around 1096; Tenochtitlán was founded in 1325.
Hiraeth (Welsh): a homesickness for a home you cannot return to — or never had. The word fuses longing, grief, and love into a single feeling English has never managed to name.
Sonder (coined 2012): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. It spread so fast it now appears in translation in a dozen languages.
On this day in 1783, the first untethered human balloon flight lifted over Paris. French gave us montgolfière for the craft — a word that briefly threatened to replace 'balloon' entirely.
Apricity: the warmth of winter sun on your skin. The word appeared in English in 1623 and then, without explanation, vanished from dictionaries. It deserves its return.
On this day in 1694, Voltaire was born. His pen name was a deliberate anagram of 'Arouet l.j.' — the 'l.j.' standing for le jeune, the young. He chose the alias after his first imprisonment.
On this date in 2021, Bitcoin hit its then-all-time high of $68,789. That peak came exactly 13 years after Satoshi published the whitepaper — an accident of the calendar, but a memorable one.

On Nov 21, 2022, Binance walked away from its FTX rescue deal after one day of due diligence. The collapse that followed erased $8B in customer funds and ended Sam Bankman-Fried's carefully constructed reputation.

Bitcoin's timechain has never produced two blocks with identical timestamps — but it legally can. The protocol only requires each block's timestamp exceed the median of the prior 11, not the previous block.
The DAO hack in 2016 didn't exploit Solidity — it exploited a re-entrancy pattern the Ethereum team had documented as dangerous months earlier. The attacker read the warnings; most developers didn't.

Satoshi's genesis block contains the headline 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' not as metadata but embedded in the coinbase transaction — unspendable text permanently inscribed in every full node on earth.

On this date in 2022, ChatGPT launched publicly. It reached 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any consumer product in history — and forced every major tech company to accelerate or abandon multi-year roadmaps.

On this date in 2023, OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman. He was reinstated 5 days later after ~700 of 770 employees threatened to quit, exposing how fragile governance structures are when talent concentration is extreme.
GPT-4 was trained on roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs for an estimated 90–100 days. The electricity alone cost more than most nations spend annually on scientific research.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — nearly every catalogued protein on Earth — in roughly 18 months. Structural biologists had manually solved ~170,000 in the prior 50 years.

The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hopfield and Hinton for work done in the 1980s. The prize committee effectively awarded foundational ML research, marking the first time the physics Nobel recognized work with no physics application.
